PDF page 9, printed page 6: two arrows connect an original X post and its reply to a reused Instagram overlay and caption. The lesson is to reuse proven material in another format, not merely copy a photo. The small tracker below has Name, Hook, Views and Link columns; surrounding text says to keep separate platform tabs. Interpretation: retain the original result and source link, then test the adaptation on its own platform. A historical example is not a guarantee that a reused caption will win.

PDF page 10, printed page 7: screenshot pairs adapt a filming formula title into offer/pricing ideas, and a memory-system title into an outlearning-system title. These illustrate the 20% winner-adjacent outlier bucket: borrow the structure from a promising idea in another niche, then change the subject and claim to fit. Interpretation: the pictured creators, titles and view counts are examples, not the user's identity or proof. The screenshots do not establish that every adapted title will work.

PDF page 13, printed page 10: the winning hook distribution pie chart divides 121 selected top hooks into statements 47.9%, commands 21.5%, questions 9.9%, exclamations 9.1%, lists 5.8%, stories 3.3% and conditionals 2.5%. The small story and conditional labels overlap slightly but belong to distinct slices. The preceding paragraphs say these were top content, ad, post and email hooks, selected by views or performance. Interpretation: this is the composition of a selected winner set, not success rates by hook type. The total number of attempts in each category is not supplied, so 47.9% is not the chance a statement succeeds or a prescribed test budget.

Physical PDF page 17: the raster callout says a free and a premium acquisition strategy must each fit across price, prospect, process, promotion and product. It argues that if premium lead costs are 5–10 times higher, price must be at least 5–10 times higher, and the offer must be worth more. The prose below explicitly says free is not right for every offer every time. Interpretation: this is a draft author's comparison, not a complete profit equation. Price and lead-cost multiples alone cannot establish equal profit when close rates, delivery cost, refunds or later sales differ. Retain those conditions when using the example.

Physical PDF page 20: the raster callout attributes some paid-versus-free lead differences to salesperson conviction, not an inherent difference in buyer willingness. The author reports four local tests and conditions the same close-rate claim on the same funnel and sales setting. Below, a discounted first purchase leads into a two-step sale and a later appointment. Interpretation: the callout is a source-reported local result, not proof that all salespeople or free and paid leads convert equally. No-show percentages and card/fee examples elsewhere on this page are not universal outcomes or authorization to charge a customer.

Physical PDF page 22 contains two raster callouts. The first explains a two-step sale: an earlier small purchase or meeting can build trust before the main sale. The second protects scarce expert time by giving the initial preparation to a front desk worker or assistant, then booking qualified people with the expert. In the dental example, preparation includes forms, X-rays and finance pre-approval; it is an example subject to real staff scope, not a universal delegation checklist. The final paragraph names a five minute appointment method: the doctor may briefly say hello and arrange the deeper visit. OCR can confuse the 5 with S and drop the word 'not' in the instruction not to give away the doctor's time. Interpretation: reducing expert time per first visit is the mechanism; neither a no-show fee nor extra steps guarantees a sale.

PDF page 20, printed page 17: the Amazon review gallery rating header reads 4.9 / 5.0; OCR may turn the 5.0 into 6.0. The second row repeats some cards from the first row, with cropped cards at the edges. Interpretation: repeated display cards are not additional unique reviewers. The prose calls for understandable numbers, collection method and date, truthful reporting and regular milestone data. Its business examples are explicitly dated July 2024 and describe that source's populations; they are not current or user-business results.

PDF page 21, printed page 18: a hand-drawn remote gym overhead sketch compares an old high-overhead gym with a new low-overhead remote gym. Similar-height tall bars sit beside high versus low shorter bars; the labeled profit gap grows when overhead falls. There are no numeric axis units or measured dollar values. Interpretation: it illustrates how lower cost can leave more profit; it cannot support a specific percentage or dollar lift. The 3.1x portfolio EBITDA claim in the preceding paragraph is separate prose, not a number measured by this sketch. Below, familiar metaphors help explain a new concept; they do not replace evidence.

PDF and printed page 31: the upper paragraph continues a price objection script with a burn-the-boats metaphor, full commitment and a strong success claim. This paragraph is partly lost in native extraction. Lower scripts compare price with support/value, ask whether a cheaper price would seem believable, and use a hypothetical extra $10,000 per month. Interpretation: these are example selling words, not evidence that financial strain causes success or a license to promise it. Keep commitment, affordability, actual support and proved outcomes separate. The hypothetical income and sample proof counts must not become the user's claims.

PDF and printed page 35: Good Fast Cheap appears as prose describing a value triangle, not as a drawn triangle in this edition. The script says to choose two and argues that buying a poor cheap option, regretting it and buying again can cost more. A lower section responds to requests for a discount with a joking higher-price answer. Interpretation: this is a price-objection example, not measured proof that every cheap rival fails or that a higher price ensures quality. Native extraction omits much of the opening paragraph despite its text quality label. Read the actual image for the full argument; do not invent a missing figure or import the next page's terms.

PDF page 13, printed page 10: three social posts pair informal founder photos with gym-owner callouts. The first two use the same opening caption beneath different photos: a family scene and a superhero costume. The dental-chair image uses a smile hook tied to lead-cost and offer claims in the pictured caption. Interpretation: these show how an ordinary founder photo and relevant words can become ad material. They do not isolate the photo's effect or prove a general lift. Screenshot claims and identities belong to the examples, not the user's business. Some captions are visibly cut off by a See more link.

PDF page 14, printed page 11: four social-post examples pair customer or community photos with identity, shared beliefs, revenue and family-time angles. Nicole's caption explicitly says she was profitable before working with the business, was not struggling and had a good team/culture. Other examples show a gym-owner gathering, a two-location revenue story and a father holding children beside a pricing story. Interpretation: an honest before-state need not be a crisis; do not rewrite Nicole as failing. These are selected ad examples with partly collapsed captions, not controlled case-study datasets or proof that one pictured event caused the result.

PDF page 25, printed page 22: the image-only results template asks for start and current monthly members, monthly revenue, monthly profit and weekly work hours. The start block also asks for the moment of change; the current block asks for the best personal moment. XXX, XX and YYY are blank placeholders, not measured results. The surrounding checklist asks for a video, the raw file, the prior best example and the six-point testimonial script. Interpretation: collect comparable before/after numbers and the person's lived change; do not infer a result from an empty template.

Physical PDF page 119: handwritten daily outreach math and activity measures compare reach-outs, content pieces and media dollars per day. A four-part grid shows manual outreach, automated outreach, organic media and paid media. Lower arrows extend customer acquisition through employees, affiliates and customers. The original handwriting states $5000 / 30 = $175 per day; that is an original arithmetic error, not OCR damage. Correct division is about $166.67 per day. It also uses $1000 / $25 per hour = 40 and rounds $1000 / $15 per hour to 66 hours (about 66.67 exactly). Interpretation: compare time and money on matching units and recheck the math; retain the original image unchanged rather than silently fixing the source.

Physical PDF page 248: the golden ratio divides percent of clients referred by percent churned and aims above one. The referral growth equation subtracts monthly percent churned from monthly percent referred. Beneath it, arrows show activate, testimonial, refer and ascend, with an explicit note that order may vary. Interpretation: growth math needs acquired referred customers and lost customers on the same base and time window; a referred prospect alone is not a new customer. Division is undefined at zero churn, though net additions can still be calculated. The picture does not make one milestone order mandatory or make positive gross referrals proof of net growth.

Physical PDF page 262: the performance diamond places performance in the center, communication at the top (1), training at the left (2), motivation at the right (3) and circumstances at the bottom (4). Arrows link the four factors with performance. Interpretation: a poor result can call for checking the clarity of the task, skill, reason to act and working conditions. The diagram alone does not prove laziness, identify one cause, or prescribe firing someone; look for evidence before choosing the fix.
Cover names the Marketing Roadmap. This is not one of the ten Scaling Roadmaps.
Six-stage map: Legitimize, Publicize, Maximize, Systematize, Industrialize, Magnetize. Marketing maturity, not company size, defines the stage.
Attention becomes money through a money model. Knowing the business exists and believing its promise are two useful demand questions; the book-launch awareness example is an anecdote.
Four rules: volume, truth, proof and efficiency. Clear third-grade writing saves reader effort. Large activity multiples are motivational source claims, not measured universal sales multipliers.

The diagnostic table checks delivery capacity, affordability, customer value and sales conversion. Its right-column NO heading conflicts with row2's explicit IF YOU CAN conditional. This conflict is visible in the original page, not an extraction fault.
Choose the first stage whose actual symptoms fit. Typical headcount and revenue are examples, not sufficient evidence of marketing maturity.

Core Three groups ads, content and outreach. Fix the offer, volume, creative and targeting before reflexively switching platforms. This grouping does not erase warm versus cold outreach or the Core Four in Leads.

More, Better, New: add useful reps, learn and improve, then repeat. A new channel can fit saturation, decline or a better risk-adjusted return. One hundred minutes OR actions are alternative activity guides.
Stage1 opener introduces Legitimize and its proof problem.
Unknown strangers lack a reason to believe. A strong claim needs visible results, not louder words.

Start with warm contacts, deliver results and document them. The source suggests free or steeply discounted work for evidence; that is not permission to buy positive public reviews or bypass a platform's review rules.
The proof exchange bundles a result, review and footage as an intended offer, not a guaranteed outcome. Establish permission for use and recording. Ad-credit availability is not verified by this PDF.
Stage1 exit signs: real numbers, checkable stories and testimonials, warm awareness and a visible posting pulse.
Stage2 opener introduces Publicize and making steady demand.
Marketing only when work is quiet creates a feast-or-famine cycle. Consistent activity is the intended fix, not a promise to eliminate every seasonal swing.
Pick one primary method and do the work. Lead magnets can reveal a problem, offer a trial or solve one part. Email and a light content pulse can support the main method.
More useful reps feed learning. Email can be valuable but is not literally free after tools, labor and permission requirements; source revenue-share claims are not forecasts.

Stage2 exit signs include weekly leads for eight-plus weeks, an activity habit, a lead magnet, a weekly list and known time or cash cost per lead. The eight-week guide is not a ban on earlier useful improvements.
Stage3 opener introduces Maximize and customer economics.
Cheap leads do not fix weak customer value. Compare the cost of a customer with profit, not just revenue.

Recurring lifetime revenue equals monthly price divided by monthly churn only with aligned periods and suitable stable assumptions. Multiply by gross margin for gross-profit LTV. Steady-state sales ceilings are not next-month cash. The meal example loses eight dollars after ten dollars of ads despite twenty dollars of revenue.

Potential levers: price, a useful premium, retention, better-fit buyers and prepay. Close-rate price bands are test ideas. Early wins and personal contact are onboarding examples. Prepaid cash still owes future service.

A three-to-one lifetime gross-profit-to-CAC ratio is a guide; cash must still cover acquisition. The service-margin target is not universal. Raising gross margin67 to80 does not itself prove twice the profit.
Stage4 opener introduces Systematize and a repeatable test process.
Separate finding winners from scaling winners. Founder-dependent ad creation is an operating limit even if ads work today.

Test angles and formats with separate lanes and optimize for a reliable downstream action. The printed kill rule says ad cost at least three times target CPQL without defining spend versus unit cost or outcomes. Do not invent the missing denominator or kill a profitable ad solely because cumulative spend grew.

Seventy-thirty budgets presume proven winners and differ from Hooks' creative-effort buckets. Daily25% spend increases, ad-count quotas and recovery stories are examples, not safe universal spending instructions. Preston's named advice is credited separately.
Stage4 exit signs: repeatable tests, decision rules, winners, a weekly review and production help. The first suggested roles are not mandatory hires before low-cost process work.
Stage5 opener introduces Industrialize and creative production capacity.
Hooks, bodies and calls to action combine into many assets. Preserve the multiplication and the assumed option counts. More variants of a real winner do not guarantee new winners.

Turn reliable human work into documented processes before using agents. Reuse captured work with permission. AI output multiples and flawless-agent language are source claims, not verified guarantees. Maddox is credited for the process quotation.

Link content and sales data to customer quality, not just views. A second channel becomes a larger priority after a repeatable engine; page8 still allows earlier exceptions. Referrals and affiliates also appear, so Core Three is a grouping, not a denial of other routes.
Stage5 exit signs: larger repeatable production, qualified demand, sales feedback and measured channels. Ten-times output is relative to a baseline and is not proof of ten-times value.
Stage6 opener introduces Magnetize and earned brand demand.

Brand trust can make later selling easier. The bank-account metaphor is an explanation, not a financial guarantee. Stand for one useful promise and show credible proof; do not freeze failed positioning.

Free useful information, repeat exposure and longer interaction can build trust. Portfolio measurement complements direct attribution but does not prove unseen brand causality. The brand quote is explicitly labeled paraphrased in the original, not verbatim Alex speech.
Start a small brand pulse by Stage2; large-scale brand focus is not a requirement to wait until100 employees. Stage6 is ongoing rather than a final graduation.
Summary repeats proof, steady reach, customer economics, tests, production and brand. It is a stage map, not six simultaneous tasks.
Choose one high-return move for the actual limit, do useful daily work and review weekly. No fixed quota or outcome is guaranteed.
Closing workshop invitation is commercial context, not a required purchase or an instruction to book anything.
